title: Week 48 Listening: In-Depth Discussion and Four-Skill Retest
instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，非官方雅思试题，也不代表任何官方分数。请先通读听力文稿，再完成40道听力题。听力共四个部分，每部分10题，题目顺序与录音内容顺序一致。填空题答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。所有解析为中文，证据为英文原文引用。
transcript:
SECTION 1: Social Dialogue

[Man] Hi, is this the right place for the community garden meeting? I saw the notice on the library board and wasn't sure which room it was in. The library seemed busy tonight, so I wanted to check before wandering around.
[Woman] Yes, come in. You must be Daniel. I'm Priya, the volunteer coordinator. We're in the small hall at the back tonight because the main room is being painted. It's a bit cramped, but we manage.
[Man] That's right. Sorry I'm a bit late — the bus was delayed. There was an accident on the high street and everything was held up for about fifteen minutes.
[Woman] No problem. We're just getting started. So, you're interested in helping with the vegetable beds? We always need more hands for those.
[Man] Yes, I've never grown anything before, but I'd like to learn. My flat only has a small balcony, so I don't have much space of my own.
[Woman] That's fine. We have raised beds, so you don't need to bend too much. Have you done any gardening at all? Even a little experience helps.
[Man] Well, my grandmother had a garden when I was a child, but I only watched. I didn't actually do anything. She did all the digging and planting herself.
[Woman] That's still useful experience — you know what healthy plants look like. Now, we meet every Saturday morning from nine to eleven. We start early because the beds get very hot later in the day.
[Man] Nine to eleven. And what would I be doing? I'd like to know what to expect before I commit.
[Woman] Mostly watering, weeding, and helping with the compost. We also need someone to help on the plant stall at the summer fair. That's in August, and it's one of our biggest events of the year.
[Man] I'd be happy to help with the stall. I'm quite good at talking to people. I work in a shop, so I'm used to dealing with customers all day.
[Woman] Great. We ask volunteers to come to at least two sessions a month. Does that work for you? We're flexible about which Saturdays you choose.
[Man] Yes, I think so. I work shifts, but I can usually manage Saturdays. My rota changes every few weeks, but weekends are normally free.
[Woman] Good. There's a training session next Wednesday evening at seven. It lasts about an hour. Can you make it? It covers basic tools and safety.
[Man] Wednesday at seven... I finish work at six, so yes, I can be there. It gives me time to get across town.
[Woman] Perfect. I'll send you the details by email. Oh, and bring a pair of gloves if you have them. The soil here can be rough on your hands.
[Man] Gloves. Right. Is there anything else I should bring? I don't want to turn up unprepared.
[Woman] Just yourself and some enthusiasm. We provide the tools. Everything from spades to watering cans is kept in the shed.
[Man] OK. And is there a fee to join? I've seen some groups charge for membership.
[Woman] No, it's completely free. We're funded by the local council. That's why we can keep the tools in good condition and run the training.
[Man] That's good to hear. One more thing — can I bring my nephew sometimes? He's twelve. He's very keen on the outdoors.
[Woman] Children are welcome if they're with an adult. He'll need to stay with you at all times. It's a rule we have to keep for safety.
[Man] Understood. Thanks, Priya. See you Wednesday.
[Woman] See you then, Daniel.

SECTION 2: Social Monologue

[Woman] Hello, everyone. This is a recorded message for new members of the Riverside Cycling Club. My name is Helen, and I'm the membership secretary. I'd like to explain how the club works and what you need to know before your first ride. Please listen carefully, as this covers the most common questions we receive.

First, our regular rides. We have three groups: beginners, intermediate, and advanced. Beginners ride on Sunday mornings at eight, and the route is about fifteen kilometres. Intermediate riders go on Saturday mornings at seven-thirty, covering around forty kilometres. Advanced riders meet on Wednesday evenings at six and usually ride sixty kilometres or more. You can move between groups once you feel ready — just speak to the ride leader. Nobody will pressure you to move up before you're comfortable.

Second, safety. Helmets are compulsory on all rides. You must also have working lights on your bike, even in summer, because some routes finish near dusk. We recommend bright clothing, but it's not required. If your bike needs repairs, our volunteer mechanic is at the club hut on Thursday evenings from six to eight. He can handle most basic problems on the spot.

Third, membership fees. Annual membership costs thirty pounds for adults and fifteen pounds for students. This covers insurance and club events. You can pay online or at the hut. Please don't pay the ride leader in cash — they can't accept it. This keeps our records simple and safe.

Fourth, social events. We have a monthly pub evening on the first Friday of each month, and a summer picnic in July. Details are on the club website. These events are a good way to meet other riders and ask questions in a relaxed setting.

Finally, if you have any questions, email me at the address on your welcome letter. Please don't phone the hut, as it's often unstaffed. Thank you for listening, and we look forward to seeing you on a ride soon.

SECTION 3: Academic Discussion

[Tutor] OK, let's begin. Today we're discussing your projects on urban green spaces. Maria, you looked at community gardens. What did you find?
[Maria] I found that community gardens can improve local air quality, but the effect is quite small compared to, say, reducing traffic. The main benefit seems to be social — people meet their neighbours.
[Tutor] Good point. So you're saying the social benefits are more significant than the environmental ones?
[Maria] Yes, in the gardens I studied. But I should add that the gardens were small — maybe two hundred square metres each. That may limit how far the findings can be generalised.
[Tutor] Right. James, you looked at parks. Did you find similar results?
[James] Not exactly. Large parks did show measurable cooling effects in summer — up to two degrees in the surrounding streets. But smaller parks had almost no effect.
[Tutor] So size matters for temperature. What about the cost?
[James] That's the problem. Maintaining a large park is expensive. The council spends about fifty thousand pounds a year on the central park alone.
[Tutor] And do you think that's good value?
[James] It depends. If you compare it to the health costs of heatwaves, it might be. But we don't have precise figures for that.
[Tutor] Good — you're being careful about the evidence. Now, Sofia, you looked at green roofs.
[Sofia] Yes. Green roofs can reduce energy use in buildings, especially for cooling. But they're expensive to install, and many older buildings can't support the weight.
[Tutor] So what's your overall conclusion?
[Sofia] I think green roofs are best for new buildings, where the cost can be included in the design from the start.
[Tutor] That's a reasonable inference. Now, for your reports, remember to compare your findings and explain any differences. Don't just describe each project separately.
[Maria] Should we include recommendations?
[Tutor] Yes, but base them on your evidence. If your data is limited, say so. That's all for today.

SECTION 4: Academic Lecture

[Lecturer] Good morning. Today I want to talk about the concept of 'walkability' and how it's measured. Walkability refers to how friendly an area is to walking — for example, whether there are safe pavements, crossings, and destinations within a short distance.

Researchers often use a walkability score. This is calculated from several factors: residential density, the mix of land uses, street connectivity, and retail floor area. A high score means many people live nearby, there are shops and services close together, and streets are well connected.

One well-known study found that people in highly walkable neighbourhoods walked about thirty minutes more per week than those in less walkable areas. However, the study also noted that people who already like walking may choose to live in walkable areas — so we can't be sure that walkability alone causes more walking. This is a classic problem of correlation versus causation.

Another issue is that walkability scores often ignore the quality of the walking environment. A street may be connected but have narrow, broken pavements. Some newer tools include measures of safety, shade, and seating.

So, what can cities do? First, they can improve crossings and pavements. Second, they can allow shops and services in residential areas. Third, they can reduce speed limits. None of these is expensive compared to building new roads.

To conclude, walkability is a useful concept, but it must be measured carefully. A high score doesn't guarantee a pleasant walk. Thank you.

grammar.title: 概括、比较、推测、条件与让步
grammar.explanation: 本课语法聚焦于如何概括信息（如 in general, overall）、进行比较（more significant than, compared to）、进行推测（may, might, can't be sure）、表达条件（if, unless）和让步（although, even if）。这些结构在学术讨论和口语中非常常用。
grammar.example: The main benefit seems to be social — people meet their neighbours.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: ______ the gardens were small, they still provided social benefits.
questions.explanation: 此处表示让步关系，用 Although 最合适。
questions.evidence: Although the gardens were small, they still provided social benefits.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: The social benefits are ______ significant than the environmental ones.
questions.explanation: 比较级用 more significant than。
questions.evidence: The social benefits are more significant than the environmental ones.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: We ______ be sure that walkability alone causes more walking.
questions.explanation: 表示推测“不能确定”，用 can't be sure。
questions.evidence: we can't be sure that walkability alone causes more walking.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: ______ you compare it to the health costs of heatwaves, it might be good value.
questions.explanation: 此处表示条件关系，用 If。
questions.evidence: If you compare it to the health costs of heatwaves, it might be.
